title: The Radium Dial Painters
standard_text:
Standard: Cite textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.
 Spiral: RI.6.2 central idea · RI.6.3 development · RI.6.4 word meaning · RI.6.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 770 – 870

paras.label: A
paras.text: In 1917 a factory in New Jersey hired young women to paint watch dials with a glowing green paint called Undark. The work paid well for the time, and the women were told the paint was harmless.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The glow came from radium, an element discovered twenty years earlier and still treated as a marvel. Radium appeared in toothpaste, in face cream, and in tonics sold as cures for almost anything.

paras.label: C
paras.text: To keep a fine point on the brush, the painters were taught to roll the bristles between their lips. A dial has small numbers, and a sharp tip was the only way to fill them. Each worker did this hundreds of times a day.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Radium behaves chemically like calcium, so the body files it away in bone. Within a few years the women began to lose teeth, and their jaws broke under ordinary pressure. Doctors who had never seen the pattern called it a mystery.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The company's own consultants had warned of the danger as early as 1925, and the company kept the reports quiet. When five of the women sued in 1927, the firm argued that they had contracted syphilis instead.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The women won a settlement in 1928, and the case helped build the legal idea that a worker can sue an employer for an occupational disease. The dials they painted still register on a Geiger counter today.

questions.q:
occupational disease: an illness a person gets from the work they do.
consultant: an expert a company hires to study a question and report back.
Describe the connection between the way radium behaves in the body and the injuries the women suffered.
questions.a: Radium behaves chemically like calcium, so the body files it away in bone, and that is why the women lost teeth and their jaws broke under ordinary pressure.

note: RI.6.1 asks for evidence, so push for the sentence, i.e. "the company's own consultants had warned of the danger as early as 1925." An answer that only says the company knew is not yet cited.

title: How a Glacier Moves
standard_text:
Standard: Cite textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.
 Spiral: RI.6.2 central idea · RI.6.3 development · RI.6.4 word meaning · RI.6.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 770 – 870

paras.label: A
paras.text: A glacier looks like a landscape that has stopped. Measure the same point for a year, though, and it will have traveled, sometimes a few centimeters and sometimes half a kilometer.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The motion has two parts. Ice under enough pressure deforms, with crystals sliding past one another deep in the body of the glacier, so the middle of the ice creeps forward even where the base is frozen fast.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second part is sliding. Meltwater collects underneath and lifts the ice just enough to break its grip on bedrock. A glacier with water under it can move ten times faster than one without.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Because the centre moves faster than the edges, the surface tears. The cracks are called crevasses, and they only open in the upper fifty meters or so, where the ice is brittle rather than plastic.

paras.label: E
paras.text: What a glacier carries, it eventually drops. Boulders frozen into the base scrape the rock beneath into long parallel grooves, and the ridge of rubble left at the front marks how far the ice once reached.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Those ridges are how glaciologists read the past. A moraine sitting in a valley in New York is a record of where the ice stood eighteen thousand years ago, long before anyone was there to measure it.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A glacier looks like a landscape that has stopped. But measure one point for a year. It will have moved. Sometimes it moves a few centimeters. Sometimes it moves half a kilometer.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The motion has two parts. Ice under great pressure bends. Crystals slide past each other deep inside. So the middle of the ice creeps forward.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second part is sliding. Meltwater gathers underneath. It lifts the ice off the rock. Ice with water under it moves ten times faster.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The centre moves faster than the edges. So the surface tears open. These cracks are called crevasses. They form only near the top, where the ice is brittle.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A glacier drops what it carries. Boulders in the base scrape long grooves in the rock. A ridge of rubble marks how far the ice reached.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Those ridges tell scientists about the past. A moraine in a New York valley shows where the ice stood. That was eighteen thousand years ago.

questions.q: What two kinds of motion make up the movement of a glacier?
questions.a: Ice deep in the glacier deforms under pressure as crystals slide past one another, and the whole glacier slides on meltwater that lifts it off the bedrock.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. deforming) and paragraph C (i.e. sliding on meltwater).
Summarize how a glacier moves and what it leaves behind.
questions.a: A glacier creeps forward as the ice deforms under pressure and slides on meltwater beneath it. The centre moves faster than the edges, so crevasses open at the surface, and the ice scrapes grooves in the rock and leaves a ridge of rubble called a moraine.

questions.q:
crevasse: a crack that opens in the brittle upper ice of a glacier.
moraine: the ridge of rock and rubble left where the front of a glacier once stood.
Describe the connection between meltwater under a glacier and how fast it travels.
questions.a: Meltwater lifts the ice just enough to break its grip on bedrock, so a glacier with water under it can move ten times faster than one without.

note: Ask where the text actually says how fast, i.e. "a few centimeters" against "half a kilometer." Citing the range is stronger than citing one number.

title: The Library of Alexandria
standard_text:
Standard: Cite textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.
 Spiral: RI.6.2 central idea · RI.6.3 development · RI.6.4 word meaning · RI.6.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 770 – 870

paras.label: A
paras.text: Alexandria's library was not a building full of books in the modern sense. It was a collection of scrolls, perhaps several hundred thousand of them, attached to a research institution the Ptolemies paid for out of the royal treasury.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The collecting was aggressive. Ships that docked at Alexandria were searched for texts. Anything found was copied, and the official policy was to keep the original and return the copy to the owner.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Scholars worked there on salary. Eratosthenes measured the circumference of the Earth from the length of two shadows. Euclid's geometry and the first serious editions of Homer came out of the same institution.

paras.label: D
paras.text: There was no single fire. Caesar's troops burned part of the harbour district in 48 BCE, later rulers cut the scholars' funding, and the Roman emperor Aurelian destroyed the quarter the library stood in around 270 CE.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Most of the loss was quieter than any of that. Papyrus rots in humid air, and a scroll survives only as long as someone keeps copying it. When the salaries stopped, the copying stopped.

paras.label: F
paras.text: We know what is missing mostly from references. Ancient authors quote works no one has read since, which is how we know, for example, that Sophocles wrote more than a hundred plays and that seven survive.

questions.q: What happened to most of the scrolls in the library at Alexandria?
questions.a: Most were lost quietly rather than in a fire, because papyrus rots in humid air and a scroll survives only as long as someone keeps copying it. When the salaries stopped, the copying stopped.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. how the scrolls were collected) and paragraph E (i.e. how they were lost).
Summarize what the library at Alexandria was and how it disappeared.
questions.a: It was a collection of several hundred thousand scrolls attached to a research institution paid for by the Ptolemies, where scholars such as Eratosthenes and Euclid worked on salary. Fire and war damaged it, but most of it was lost because the copying stopped.

questions.q:
papyrus: the plant-based writing material ancient scrolls were made from.
circumference: the distance around the outside of a circle or a sphere.
Describe the connection between paying scholars a salary and the survival of the scrolls.
questions.a: Scholars worked there on salary and the scrolls survived only as long as someone kept copying them, so when the funding was cut the copying stopped and the collection decayed.

note: A good citation here is specific, i.e. "the official policy was to keep the original and return the copy." Students often paraphrase that into something vaguer and lose the detail.

title: What a Crow Remembers
standard_text:
Standard: Cite textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.
 Spiral: RI.6.2 central idea · RI.6.3 development · RI.6.4 word meaning · RI.6.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 770 – 870

paras.label: A
paras.text: A crow that has been treated badly by a person does not forget. Researchers at the University of Washington tested this by wearing a particular rubber mask while trapping and banding wild crows on campus.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Afterwards the scientists walked the same paths in the same mask. The crows scolded them, dived at them, and recruited other birds to mob the mask, even birds that had never been trapped.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Walking the same route in a different mask produced nothing at all. The crows were not reacting to the people underneath, or to the act of walking, or to being watched. They were reacting to a face.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The behavior spread through the flock. Young crows hatched after the trapping scolded the mask as well, which means they had learned who to distrust from the adults around them rather than from any experience of their own.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Five years later the mask still drew a crowd, and the number of birds responding had grown. The researchers had to retire the mask, because it had become useless as a control.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The finding matters beyond crows. An animal that holds a grudge across generations is managing information about specific individuals, and that kind of social memory was long assumed to require a much larger brain than a crow has.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A crow that has been treated badly does not forget. Scientists at a university tested this. They wore a rubber mask while they trapped and banded wild crows.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Later the scientists walked the same paths in the same mask. The crows scolded them and dived at them. Other crows joined in. Some had never been trapped.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Then they walked the route in a different mask. Nothing happened. The crows were not upset by the people. They were upset by a face.

paras.label: D

paras.label: E
paras.text: Five years later the mask still drew a crowd. More birds joined each time. The scientists had to retire the mask.

paras.label: F
paras.text: This matters beyond crows. The birds keep track of one individual face. Scientists once thought that took a much larger brain.

questions.q: How did the researchers show that the crows were reacting to a face and not to the people?
questions.a: They walked the same route in a different mask and nothing happened at all, so the crows were not reacting to the people underneath or to the act of walking.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. the second mask) and paragraph D (i.e. the young crows).
Summarize what the mask experiment showed about crows.
questions.a: Researchers trapped and banded crows while wearing a particular mask, and afterwards the crows scolded and mobbed anyone wearing it. A different mask drew no response, and young crows hatched later scolded it too, so the birds remember a specific face and pass the warning on.

questions.q:
mob: to gather and harass a predator or a threat as a group.
band: to fit a bird with a numbered ring so it can be identified later.
Describe the connection between the young crows' behavior and what the adults taught them.
questions.a: Young crows hatched after the trapping scolded the mask although they had never been trapped, so they had learned who to distrust from the adults around them rather than from their own experience.

note: The strongest evidence here is the control, i.e. "walking the same route in a different mask produced nothing at all." Students tend to cite the diving crows instead, which on its own proves less.

title: The Pullman Porters
standard_text:
Standard: Cite textual evidence to support analysis of what the text says explicitly as well as inferences drawn from the text.
 Spiral: RI.6.2 central idea · RI.6.3 development · RI.6.4 word meaning · RI.6.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 770 – 870

paras.label: A
paras.text: From the 1870s the Pullman Company staffed its sleeping cars almost entirely with Black men, many of them formerly enslaved. The job came with a uniform, a national route, and wages low enough that porters depended on tips.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Passengers often called any porter George, after George Pullman, rather than learning a name. The company did not discourage it. A porter who objected could be reported, and a reported porter could be fired without explanation.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The work was still sought after. A porter earned steady money, saw the country, and carried home newspapers and ideas from cities his neighbours would never visit. Porters' children went to college in unusual numbers.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Organizing took twelve years. A. Philip Randolph founded the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters in 1925, and the company fought it with spies, firings, and a rival union of its own making.

paras.label: E
paras.text: In 1937 Pullman signed. It was the first contract between a major American corporation and a union led by Black workers, and it cut the porters' hours and raised their pay.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The Brotherhood outlasted the sleeping car. Its members organized the 1941 march that pushed Roosevelt to ban discrimination in defence plants, and Randolph was still at the front of the march on Washington in 1963.

questions.q: Why did the porters depend on tips?
questions.a: The Pullman Company paid wages low enough that porters had to rely on tips from passengers.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. being called George) and paragraph E (i.e. the 1937 contract).

questions.a: They were Black men who staffed Pullman sleeping cars from the 1870s for low wages and tips. After twelve years of organizing, the Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters won a contract in 1937, the first between a major American corporation and a union led by Black workers, and its members went on to organize marches for civil rights.

questions.q:
porter: a railway worker who served passengers in a sleeping car.
brotherhood: a name many early unions used for themselves.
Describe the connection between the porters' national route and what they brought home.
questions.a: A porter saw the country on the job, so he carried home newspapers and ideas from cities his neighbours would never visit.

note: Both things in paragraph C are true at once: the job was demeaning and it was sought after. Ask students to cite a sentence for each side rather than choosing one.

title: Why the Ocean Is Salty
standard_text:
Standard: Determine a central idea of a text and how it is conveyed through particular details; provide a summary of the text distinct from personal opinions or judgments.
 Spiral: RI.6.1 citing evidence · RI.6.3 development · RI.6.5 structure · RI.6.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 770 – 870

paras.label: A
paras.text: Rain is fresh, rivers are fresh, and almost all the water in the ocean arrived by one of those two routes. The obvious question is where the salt came from, and the answer is that the rivers brought it.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Rain is faintly acidic, because carbon dioxide from the air dissolves into it. Falling on rock, it breaks the rock down slowly and carries off dissolved ions, including the sodium and chloride that make up table salt.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A river tastes fresh because the concentration is low. The Mississippi carries about a tenth of a gram of dissolved salt per litre, which no tongue can detect, and delivers it to the Gulf of Mexico every second of every year.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The ocean has no outlet. Water leaves it by evaporating, and evaporation takes only the water. Everything dissolved in it stays behind, so the salt has been accumulating for something close to four billion years.

paras.label: E
paras.text: It is not accumulating without limit. Salt leaves the ocean too, in sea spray that dries on land, in minerals that settle out on the sea floor, and in the hot vents where seawater cycles through the crust and comes back altered.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Those two rates have been roughly balanced for a long time, which is why the ocean is about 35 grams of salt per litre and has been for hundreds of millions of years. The ocean is not getting saltier in any way a person would notice.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Rain is fresh. Rivers are fresh. Almost all the ocean's water came from one of those two. So where did the salt come from? The rivers brought it.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Rain is slightly acidic. Carbon dioxide from the air dissolves into it. The rain breaks down rock. It carries off the sodium and chloride that make table salt.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A river tastes fresh because the amount is small. The Mississippi carries about a tenth of a gram per litre. No tongue can taste that. But it never stops.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The ocean has no outlet. Water leaves it by evaporating. Evaporation takes only the water. Everything dissolved in it stays behind.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Salt leaves the ocean too. Sea spray dries on land. Minerals settle on the sea floor. Hot vents in the crust take some back.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Those two rates are about equal. So the ocean holds about 35 grams of salt per litre. It has held that for a very long time.

questions.q: Why does salt stay in the ocean when water leaves it?
questions.a: Water leaves the ocean by evaporating, and evaporation takes only the water, so everything dissolved in it stays behind.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. why salt builds up) and paragraph E (i.e. how salt leaves again).
Summarize where the ocean's salt comes from and why it is not getting saltier.
questions.a: Slightly acidic rain breaks down rock and rivers carry the dissolved salt to the sea. The ocean has no outlet and evaporation removes only water, so salt accumulates. But salt also leaves in sea spray, in minerals on the sea floor, and through hot vents, and the two rates are roughly balanced.

questions.q:
ion: a dissolved particle carrying an electric charge, such as the sodium and chloride in salt.
concentration: how much of a substance is dissolved in a given amount of water.
Describe the connection between a river tasting fresh and the ocean tasting salty.
questions.a: A river carries only about a tenth of a gram of salt per litre, too little for a tongue to detect, but it delivers that salt every second of every year and the ocean keeps all of it.

note: The central idea is the balance, not the build-up. A summary that stops at "rivers bring salt" has taken half the text, which is worth naming.

title: The Women Who Computed Orbits
standard_text:
Standard: Determine a central idea of a text and how it is conveyed through particular details; provide a summary of the text distinct from personal opinions or judgments.
 Spiral: RI.6.1 citing evidence · RI.6.3 development · RI.6.5 structure · RI.6.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 770 – 870

paras.label: A
paras.text: Before computer meant a machine, it meant a person doing arithmetic for a living. NASA's predecessor employed rooms of them, and at the Langley laboratory in Virginia a group of Black women worked as computers in a segregated wing called West Area Computing.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The work was mathematics, not clerical. A computer took raw numbers from a wind tunnel or a flight test and ran them through equations by hand, with a slide rule and a mechanical calculator, until they became something an engineer could use.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Katherine Johnson moved from that pool into a flight research group and stayed. She calculated the trajectory for Alan Shepard's 1961 flight and the launch window for the mission that put him in the air.

paras.label: D
paras.text: When Glenn's orbital flight was programmed on an IBM machine in 1962, he asked for Johnson to check the computer's numbers by hand before he would fly. She did, and the figures agreed.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Dorothy Vaughan read the same situation differently. Seeing that the machines were coming, she taught herself Fortran, taught it to the women in her group, and moved the whole unit into programming rather than watch it be replaced.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Mary Jackson went a third way. She petitioned a Virginia court for permission to take engineering classes at a segregated white high school, won, and became NASA's first Black female engineer.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The records were public the whole time. What was missing was not the evidence but anyone assembling it, which is why the story arrived as news in 2016 rather than 1962.

paras.text: The work was mathematics, not filing. A computer took raw numbers from a flight test. She ran them through equations by hand. She used a slide rule and a mechanical calculator.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Katherine Johnson moved into a flight research group. She stayed there. She worked out the path for Alan Shepard's 1961 flight.

questions.q: What did a human computer actually do?
questions.a: A computer took raw numbers from a wind tunnel or a flight test and ran them through equations by hand, using a slide rule and a mechanical calculator, until they became something an engineer could use.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. Glenn's request) and paragraph E (i.e. Vaughan learning Fortran).
Summarize what the women of West Area Computing did at NASA.
questions.a: They worked as human computers in a segregated wing, turning raw flight data into usable figures by hand. Katherine Johnson calculated flight trajectories and checked a machine's numbers for John Glenn, Dorothy Vaughan moved her group into programming, and Mary Jackson won a court petition and became an engineer.

questions.q:
trajectory: the path an object follows through space.
segregated: kept separate by race, by law or by policy.
Describe the connection between the arrival of the IBM machines and what Dorothy Vaughan decided to do.
questions.a: Vaughan saw that the machines were coming, so she taught herself Fortran and taught it to the women in her group, moving the whole unit into programming rather than watch it be replaced.

note: The last paragraph is the central idea and students usually skip it. Ask what it means that the records were public the whole time.

title: The Lake That Flipped Over
standard_text:
Standard: Determine a central idea of a text and how it is conveyed through particular details; provide a summary of the text distinct from personal opinions or judgments.
 Spiral: RI.6.1 citing evidence · RI.6.3 development · RI.6.5 structure · RI.6.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 770 – 870

paras.label: A
paras.text: On the night of 21 August 1986, something came out of Lake Nyos in Cameroon and killed more than 1,700 people and 3,500 animals in the valleys below. Nothing burned and nothing was crushed.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Nyos sits in the crater of an old volcano. The volcano is not erupting, but carbon dioxide still seeps up from the magma beneath and dissolves into the deep water of the lake.

paras.label: C
paras.text: In most lakes that gas would escape. Water turns over seasonally, cold surface water sinking and deep water rising. Nyos is deep, tropical, and almost never turns over, so the gas stayed down and the pressure of 200 meters of water kept it dissolved.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Something disturbed the bottom layer that night, possibly a landslide. Once a pocket of deep water rose even slightly, the pressure on it dropped, bubbles formed, and the bubbling water rose faster, which dropped the pressure further.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The lake emptied about a cubic kilometer of carbon dioxide in a matter of hours. The gas is heavier than air, so it did not disperse upward. It flowed downhill, filled the valleys, and displaced the air people were breathing.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Survivors described a smell and a sound and then waking hours later beside relatives who had not. Many were unconscious before they understood anything was happening.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Engineers have since run pipes from the deep water to the surface. The lake now vents itself in a controlled fountain, slowly, instead of all at once.

questions.q: Why did the gas from the lake stay in the valleys instead of blowing away?
questions.a: Carbon dioxide is heavier than air, so it did not disperse upward. It flowed downhill, filled the valleys, and displaced the air people were breathing.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. why the gas stayed dissolved) and paragraph D (i.e. what set it free).
Summarize what happened at Lake Nyos in 1986.
questions.a: Carbon dioxide from the magma below had been dissolving into the deep water of a lake that almost never turns over. One night something disturbed the bottom layer, the gas came out of solution all at once, and about a cubic kilometer of it flowed downhill and suffocated more than 1,700 people.

questions.q:
displace: to push something out of the space it occupied, as the gas pushed out the air.
turn over: when a lake's surface water sinks and its deep water rises, mixing the two.
Describe the connection between a bubble forming in the deep water and the speed of what followed.
questions.a: Once a pocket of deep water rose even slightly the pressure on it dropped, so bubbles formed, and the bubbling water rose faster, which dropped the pressure further and emptied the lake in hours.

note: This is a runaway loop, and naming it as one is the central idea. The pipes in the last paragraph are the answer to the loop, not a separate fact.

title: The Match Girls' Strike
standard_text:
Standard: Determine a central idea of a text and how it is conveyed through particular details; provide a summary of the text distinct from personal opinions or judgments.

paras.label: A
paras.text: In July 1888, about 1,400 women and girls walked out of the Bryant and May match factory in London's East End. Most were teenagers, none had a union, and almost nobody expected them to win.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The matches were made with white phosphorus. Workers who breathed the fumes developed an abscess in the jawbone that glowed faintly in the dark and eventually destroyed the bone. The disease had a nickname: phossy jaw.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Pay was piecework and came with fines. A girl could be fined for talking, for dropping matches, for going to the toilet without permission, or for having dirty feet. The fines came out of wages already below subsistence.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A journalist named Annie Besant printed an article about the conditions, naming figures and naming the company. Bryant and May demanded that the workers sign a statement calling it untrue. They refused, a girl was dismissed, and the factory emptied.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The company expected hunger to settle it. Instead the strikers organized a fund, marched to Parliament, gave evidence to members who had never spoken to a factory worker, and kept the story in the newspapers for two weeks.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Bryant and May gave in. The fines ended, wages rose, and the workers formed the largest union of women and girls in the country.

paras.label: G
paras.text: White phosphorus took longer. Britain did not ban it in matches until 1908, twenty years after the strike, and only after a treaty made the ban international.

title: The Bones That Carry Sound
standard_text:
Standard: Determine a central idea of a text and how it is conveyed through particular details; provide a summary of the text distinct from personal opinions or judgments.
 Spiral: RI.6.1 citing evidence · RI.6.3 development · RI.6.5 structure · RI.6.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 770 – 870

paras.label: A
paras.text: A sound that reaches you has to cross from air into fluid. The inner ear is filled with liquid, and sound moving from air into water normally bounces off, losing about 99.9 percent of its energy at the boundary.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Three bones solve the problem. The malleus, incus and stapes sit in the middle ear, the smallest bones in the body, and together they bridge the eardrum and the fluid behind it.

paras.label: C
paras.text: They work by concentrating force. The eardrum is roughly twenty times the area of the oval window the stapes pushes on, so the same force arrives spread over a much smaller patch and the pressure rises enough to move liquid.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The chain also acts as a lever, which adds a little more. The combined gain is about thirty-fold, almost exactly what is needed to cancel the loss at the air-fluid boundary.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The system can protect itself. Two tiny muscles tighten against loud sound and stiffen the chain, which cuts the transmission. The reflex takes tens of milliseconds, so it defends against a long noise and not against a gunshot.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Evolution built this out of spare parts. In reptiles two of these three bones are part of the jaw joint, and the fossil record shows them migrating into the ear across tens of millions of years as the mammal jaw simplified.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Surgeons now replace a damaged chain with a prosthesis. The replacement does not have to look like a bone. It has to deliver the same thirty-fold gain.

stapes: the last of the three middle ear bones, the one that pushes on the oval window.

title: The Doctor Nobody Believed
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze in detail how a key individual, event, or idea is introduced, illustrated, and elaborated in a text, including through examples or anecdotes.
 Spiral: RI.6.1 citing evidence · RI.6.2 central idea · RI.6.5 structure · RI.6.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 770 – 870

paras.label: A
paras.text: In 1846 the Vienna General Hospital ran two maternity clinics side by side. In the first, where medical students delivered babies, about one mother in ten died of childbed fever. In the second, staffed by midwives, the rate was closer to one in twenty-five.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Women in the city knew the numbers. Some begged to be sent to the second clinic. Some gave birth in the street rather than go to the first, and those street births had a lower death rate than the ward.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Ignaz Semmelweis, a young assistant, tried to find a difference he could test. He ruled out crowding, ruled out climate, and ruled out the position women lay in, because changing them changed nothing.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The answer came from a death. A colleague cut his finger during an autopsy and died with exactly the symptoms the mothers had. Semmelweis saw what the students did that the midwives did not: they came to the ward from the dissecting room.

paras.label: E
paras.text: He ordered hand washing in chlorinated lime. Deaths in the first clinic fell from about eighteen percent to around two within a year. He had no germ theory to explain it and called the cause cadaverous particles.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The profession rejected him. Washing hands implied that doctors were carrying death from bed to bed, and senior physicians treated the suggestion as an insult. His contract was not renewed.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Semmelweis died in an asylum in 1865, of an infected wound. Lister published on antiseptic surgery two years later, and Pasteur's work soon gave the explanation Semmelweis had never had.

title: The Idea Called Plate Tectonics
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze in detail how a key individual, event, or idea is introduced, illustrated, and elaborated in a text, including through examples or anecdotes.
 Spiral: RI.6.1 citing evidence · RI.6.2 central idea · RI.6.5 structure · RI.6.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 770 – 870

paras.label: A
paras.text: Look at a world map and South America appears to fit into Africa. People noticed the fit within decades of accurate coastlines being drawn, and for three centuries it was treated as a coincidence.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Alfred Wegener took it seriously. In 1912 he assembled the fit of the coasts, matching rock formations on both sides, and identical fossils of animals that could not have swum an ocean, and argued that the continents had once been joined.

paras.label: C
paras.text: His argument had a hole. He could not say what moved a continent, and his suggestion that they ploughed through the ocean floor was physically impossible. Geologists rejected the whole idea on the strength of that one weakness.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The evidence arrived from the sea. Sonar surveys after 1945 mapped a mountain ridge running down the middle of the Atlantic, with a valley along its crest, which nobody had predicted.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Then came the stripes. The Earth's magnetic field reverses every so often, and the rock on either side of the ridge is magnetised in matching bands, like a tape recording running outward in both directions from the centre.

paras.label: F
paras.text: That gave the mechanism Wegener lacked. New sea floor is made at the ridge and spreads outward, carrying the continents with it, so they do not plough through the ocean floor. They ride on it.

paras.label: G
paras.text: By 1968 the idea had a name and a map of a dozen plates. The fit of the coastlines had been right for three hundred years, and it took a mechanism before anyone would accept it.

title: The House on Halsted Street
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze in detail how a key individual, event, or idea is introduced, illustrated, and elaborated in a text, including through examples or anecdotes.
 Spiral: RI.6.1 citing evidence · RI.6.2 central idea · RI.6.5 structure · RI.6.10 comprehension

paras.label: A
paras.text: Jane Addams was twenty-nine and had no plan she could name when she rented a worn mansion on Halsted Street in Chicago in 1889. The neighbourhood around it held immigrants from nineteen countries.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The idea was to live there. Addams and Ellen Gates Starr moved in rather than visiting to deliver charity, which was how most relief worked at the time, and the distinction mattered to the neighbours more than anything else they did.

paras.label: C
paras.text: What Hull House became was decided by what people asked for. A kindergarten came first, because mothers working in sweatshops had nowhere to leave children. A night school followed, then a gymnasium, a public bath, a labour museum and a theatre.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The residents also counted things. They mapped wages and nationalities street by street and published the figures, and those maps were among the first pieces of American social research built from door-to-door data.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The counting turned into law. Hull House residents drafted and pushed an Illinois factory inspection act in 1893, and later work from the house fed into the first juvenile court in the country and into limits on child labour.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Addams took the same approach to war and lost most of her reputation for it. Her opposition to American entry into the First World War had her called unpatriotic and watched by federal agents.

paras.label: G
paras.text: She received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1931, four years before she died. Hull House itself kept running as a settlement until 1963, and its buildings are now a museum.

title: The Box That Changed Trade
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze in detail how a key individual, event, or idea is introduced, illustrated, and elaborated in a text, including through examples or anecdotes.
 Spiral: RI.6.1 citing evidence · RI.6.2 central idea · RI.6.5 structure · RI.6.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 770 – 870

paras.label: A
paras.text: Before 1956, loading a ship meant moving each thing separately. Crates, sacks, barrels and bales came down to the dock, and gangs of longshoremen stowed them by hand in whatever shape the hold allowed.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It was slow and it was most of the cost. Cargo might sit on a pier for weeks, and moving goods by sea could take up to a quarter of the value of the goods themselves.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Malcom McLean was a trucking operator, not a shipowner. He had spent years watching his drivers wait at docks and concluded that the answer was to stop unloading trucks at all and put the whole trailer body on the ship.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The first voyage carried fifty-eight boxes from Newark to Houston in April 1956. The loading cost fell from about $5.83 a ton to sixteen cents, a figure so far outside expectations that it was checked repeatedly.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The box only worked once everyone used the same box. McLean released his patents, and a decade of argument produced a standard length, standard corner fittings and a standard lifting point, which is why a container from any port fits any crane.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Whole industries followed the change. Factories could sit far from the customer, ports that could not take a crane declined, and the longshore workforce in most cities shrank by more than half.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The box itself is unremarkable. Its importance is that a shipping line, a railway, a crane and a truck all agreed on one set of measurements and stopped touching the cargo.

title: The Mold on the Windowsill
standard_text:

paras.label: A
paras.text: Alexander Fleming came back from holiday in September 1928 to a stack of dishes he had left out. One of them, growing Staphylococcus, had been contaminated by a mold, and around the mold the bacteria had cleared away.

paras.label: B
paras.text: He had noticed a version of this before. Four years earlier a drop from his own nose had landed on a plate and cleared a patch, which led him to an enzyme in tears and saliva called lysozyme.

paras.label: C
paras.text: So he recognized the pattern. He grew the mold, identified it as a Penicillium, tested the fluid it released against several bacteria, and published the result in 1929 under a title almost nobody read.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Then it stalled for ten years. Fleming could not extract the active substance in any useful amount, and he was a bacteriologist rather than a chemist. He mostly moved on to other work.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Howard Florey and Ernst Chain picked the paper up at Oxford in 1938. Their contribution was not the discovery but the extraction, and it took a team, a freeze-drying apparatus and bathtubs' worth of mold broth to produce a few grams.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The first patient was a policeman with an infected scratch. He improved for five days and then died, because the supply ran out. The team had been recovering penicillin from his urine to stretch it.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Scale was solved in America, in wartime, with a strain of Penicillium found on a cantaloupe in an Illinois market. By 1944 there was enough for the invasion of Europe, sixteen years after the dish.

questions.q: Why did the first patient treated with penicillin die?
questions.a: He improved for five days and then died because the supply ran out, even though the team had been recovering penicillin from his urine to stretch it.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. the earlier plate) and paragraph E (i.e. the extraction at Oxford).
Summarize how penicillin went from a contaminated dish to a usable drug.
questions.a: Fleming found a mold clearing bacteria on a dish in 1928, grew it, tested it and published, but could not extract the active substance. Florey and Chain solved the extraction at Oxford ten years later, and American wartime production using a strain found on a cantaloupe made enough for the invasion of Europe by 1944.

questions.q:
contaminated: having something unwanted land in or on it.
extraction: separating a wanted substance out of the mixture it is in.
Describe the connection between Fleming's earlier work on the nose drop and what he did with the mold.
questions.a: A drop from his own nose had cleared a patch on a plate four years earlier and led him to lysozyme, so he recognized the pattern when the mold cleared the bacteria and grew it instead of discarding the dish.

note: Three people are introduced and the text is careful about what each did, i.e. "their contribution was not the discovery but the extraction." That sentence is the one to analyse.

title: What a Cone of Uncertainty Means
standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including figurative, connotative, and technical meanings.
 Spiral: RI.6.1 citing evidence · RI.6.2 central idea · RI.6.6 point of view · RI.6.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 770 – 870

paras.label: A
paras.text: A hurricane forecast arrives as a map with a white cone spreading out from the storm. Almost everyone reads the cone as the area the hurricane will damage, and almost everyone is wrong.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The cone shows where the centre of the storm is likely to be. It is drawn so that the centre stays inside it about two thirds of the time, which means the centre falls outside the cone in roughly one forecast out of three.

paras.label: C
paras.text: It says nothing at all about size. A storm's damaging wind can extend two hundred miles from the centre, so the dangerous area is often far wider than the cone, and a town outside the white shape can still be flattened.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The word uncertainty is doing specific work here. In ordinary speech it suggests the forecasters are unsure, which sounds like weakness. In forecasting it is a measured quantity, calculated from how far past forecasts have missed.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Other words on the same map are technical too. A watch means conditions are possible within forty-eight hours; a warning means they are expected within thirty-six. The two words are not stronger and weaker versions of each other.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Forecasters have tried to fix the misreading by renaming things. Nothing has worked well, partly because a cone is such a natural shape to read as a beam of damage spreading outward.

paras.label: G
paras.text: So the fix has been to publish other maps alongside it, showing wind arrival times and surge depths. The cone is accurate. What it means is simply not what it looks like.

paras.label: G
paras.text: So they publish other maps beside it. Those show wind times and flood depths. The cone is accurate. It just does not mean what it looks like.

questions.q: What does the cone on a hurricane map actually show?
questions.a: It shows where the centre of the storm is likely to be, drawn so that the centre stays inside it about two thirds of the time.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. the word uncertainty) and paragraph E (i.e. watch and warning).
Summarize what the cone of uncertainty means and why people misread it.

People read it as the damage zone because a cone looks like a beam spreading outward, so forecasters now publish wind and surge maps alongside it.

questions.q:
uncertainty: in forecasting, a measured amount calculated from how far past forecasts have missed.
surge: the rise in sea level a storm pushes onto the shore.
Describe the connection between the size of a storm's wind field and the width of the cone.
questions.a: A storm's damaging wind can extend two hundred miles from the centre while the cone only tracks the centre, so the dangerous area is often far wider than the cone.

note: The hinge is paragraph D: the same word means one thing in speech and another in forecasting. That is exactly the everyday-against-technical distinction RI.6.4 names.

title: Theory, Law, and Hypothesis
standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including figurative, connotative, and technical meanings.
 Spiral: RI.6.1 citing evidence · RI.6.2 central idea · RI.6.6 point of view · RI.6.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 770 – 870

paras.label: A
paras.text: In ordinary conversation a theory is a guess. Someone says they have a theory about why the bus is late, and nobody expects evidence. In science the word is almost the opposite of a guess.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A scientific theory is an explanation that has survived testing. The theory of plate tectonics explains earthquakes, mountain ranges and the fit of coastlines at once, and it has not been overturned by anything found since.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A hypothesis is the smaller thing. It is a specific, testable statement, usually phrased so that a single experiment could show it to be false, and most hypotheses are abandoned rather than promoted.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A law is different again, and it is not a promoted theory. A law describes what happens; a theory explains why. Newton's law of gravitation gives the number. The theory of general relativity gives the reason.

paras.label: E
paras.text: This is why the phrase just a theory does so much damage in an argument. It borrows the weakness of the everyday word and attaches it to the strongest thing science has.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Scientists make the problem worse themselves. Significant, model, error and bias all have ordinary meanings that collide with their technical ones, and error in particular does not mean mistake.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The vocabulary is not going to change. What a reader can do is notice when a word is being used as the field uses it, and when it has quietly slipped back into everyday speech.

paras.label: A
paras.text: In everyday talk a theory is a guess. Someone has a theory about the late bus. Nobody expects proof. In science the word means nearly the opposite.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A scientific theory is an explanation that has survived testing. Plate tectonics explains earthquakes and mountains and coastlines. Nothing found since has overturned it.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A hypothesis is smaller. It is one testable statement. Usually a single experiment could show it is false. Most hypotheses are abandoned.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A law is different again. It is not a promoted theory. A law describes what happens. A theory explains why. Newton's law gives the number.

paras.label: E
paras.text: This is why just a theory is unfair in an argument. It takes the weak everyday word. Then it sticks that word on the strongest thing science has.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Scientists make it worse. Significant, model, error and bias all have two meanings. Error does not mean mistake.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The words will not change. A reader can still watch for them. Notice when a word is technical and when it is ordinary.

questions.q: What is the difference between a law and a theory in science?
questions.a: A law describes what happens and a theory explains why, so Newton's law of gravitation gives the number while the theory of general relativity gives the reason.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. hypothesis) and paragraph E (i.e. the phrase just a theory).
Summarize how theory, law and hypothesis differ from each other.
questions.a: A hypothesis is one specific testable statement, usually phrased so an experiment could show it false. A theory is an explanation that has survived testing. A law describes what happens rather than why, so it is not a promoted theory.

questions.q:
hypothesis: a specific statement phrased so that a single experiment could show it to be false.
connotation: the feeling a word carries beyond its plain meaning, as guess clings to theory.
Describe the connection between the everyday meaning of theory and the phrase just a theory.
questions.a: The everyday word means a guess that nobody expects evidence for, so just a theory borrows that weakness and attaches it to the strongest thing science has.

note: Paragraph F is worth lingering on. Error not meaning mistake is the clearest case of a technical meaning a student will meet all year.

title: The Words of the Declaration
standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including figurative, connotative, and technical meanings.
 Spiral: RI.6.1 citing evidence · RI.6.2 central idea · RI.6.6 point of view · RI.6.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 770 – 870

paras.label: A
paras.text: The Declaration of Independence is a short document, and most of what it does is legal rather than poetic. It lists grievances, states a principle, and announces a decision. The famous sentence is in the second paragraph.

paras.label: B
paras.text: We hold these truths to be self-evident. Self-evident meant something precise in 1776: a statement that needs no proof because understanding it is the same as seeing that it is true. Jefferson's draft had said sacred and undeniable.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Unalienable is a legal term, not a flourish. A right that is unalienable cannot be transferred or surrendered, even by the person who holds it, which makes it a different and stronger claim than a right that is merely protected.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The pursuit of happiness replaced property, which appeared in similar lists of the period. Happiness in eighteenth-century usage meant something closer to flourishing or well-being than to a mood.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Other words have shifted so far that they mislead. Prudence in the document means careful judgment rather than caution. Suffer in the phrase about enduring evils means to allow or put up with, not to be in pain.

paras.label: F
paras.text: And men meant men. The document's principles were written by a man who held people in slavery, and the gap between the words and their application is the argument that every later movement for rights has used.

paras.label: G
paras.text: Frederick Douglass made exactly that move in 1852, asking what the Fourth of July meant to the slave and quoting the Declaration back at the country. The words were strong enough to be used against the people who wrote them.

paras.label: C

paras.label: D

paras.label: G
paras.text: Frederick Douglass did this in 1852. He asked what the Fourth of July meant to the slave. He quoted the Declaration back at the country.

questions.q: What does unalienable mean in the Declaration?
questions.a: A right that is unalienable cannot be transferred or surrendered, even by the person who holds it, which makes it a stronger claim than a right that is merely protected.

questions.q: Paragraph B (i.e. self-evident) and paragraph F (i.e. the word men).
Summarize what careful reading of the Declaration's words reveals.
questions.a: Words such as self-evident, unalienable and happiness had precise eighteenth-century meanings that are stronger or different than they sound now, and words such as prudence and suffer have shifted far enough to mislead. The gap between the document's principles and the slavery of the man who wrote them became the argument later movements used.

questions.q:
unalienable: unable to be transferred or surrendered, even by the person who holds the right.
grievance: a complaint about a wrong that has been done.
Describe the connection between the Declaration's words and the way Frederick Douglass used them.
questions.a: The words stated a principle that the country had not applied, so Douglass asked what the Fourth of July meant to the slave and quoted the Declaration back at the people who wrote it.

note: Paragraph D is a replacement, not a synonym, i.e. property became the pursuit of happiness. Ask what changes when a word is swapped rather than defined.

title: Headline Words
standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including figurative, connotative, and technical meanings.
 Spiral: RI.6.1 citing evidence · RI.6.2 central idea · RI.6.6 point of view · RI.6.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 770 – 870

paras.label: A
paras.text: A headline has to fit a column, so newspapers developed a vocabulary of short words that rarely appear anywhere else. Officials do not vow in conversation, and a disagreement only becomes a rift in print.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Length is the first reason. Probe is four letters and investigation is thirteen. Bid replaces attempt, slam replaces criticise sharply, and eye replaces is considering, which saves a line of type.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The second reason is tone. Each of those short words carries more heat than the word it replaces. A council that slams a proposal sounds angrier than one that criticises it, though the underlying quote may be identical.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Hedges go the other way. Linked to, amid, and sparked concern all suggest a relationship without claiming one, which lets a headline imply more than the article will support.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A reader can test any headline against its own article. If the headline says a study links a food to a disease, the article will usually say the study found an association in a group of people, which is a weaker statement.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Headlines are also often not written by the reporter. A copy editor working to a character count writes most of them, which is why a careful article can sit underneath an overheated line.

paras.label: G
paras.text: None of this makes headlines dishonest. It makes them a compressed form with its own conventions, and reading one as if it were a sentence from the article is the mistake.

paras.text: A headline must fit a column. So newspapers use short words. Officials do not vow in conversation. A disagreement becomes a rift only in print.

paras.label: G
paras.text: None of this makes headlines dishonest. They are a compressed form with rules. Reading one as a plain sentence is the mistake.

questions.q: Why do headlines use words such as probe and bid?
questions.a: Length is the first reason, because probe is four letters and investigation is thirteen, so the short word saves a line of type.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. tone) and paragraph D (i.e. hedges).
Summarize why headline words differ from the words in the article.
questions.a: Headlines must fit a column, so they use short words such as probe, bid and slam, and those words carry more heat than the ones they replace. Hedges such as linked to imply a relationship without claiming one, and a copy editor working to a character count usually writes the headline rather than the reporter.

questions.q:
hedge: a word that suggests a relationship without claiming one, such as linked to or amid.
association: a pattern found in a group of people, which is weaker than a cause.
Describe the connection between who writes a headline and how well it matches the article.
questions.a: A copy editor working to a character count writes most headlines rather than the reporter, which is why a careful article can sit underneath an overheated line.

note: Students can test paragraph E on a real headline in five minutes. That transfer is the point of the lesson, not the list of words.

title: What Invasive Means
standard_text:
Standard: Determine the meaning of words and phrases as they are used in a text, including figurative, connotative, and technical meanings.
 Spiral: RI.6.1 citing evidence · RI.6.2 central idea · RI.6.6 point of view · RI.6.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 770 – 870

paras.label: A
paras.text: Invasive is a technical term with a military word inside it, and the metaphor does real work. It suggests an attacker arriving with intent, which is not how a plant or a fish moves anywhere.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The technical definition has two parts. A species must be non-native to the place, and it must cause harm there, to the ecosystem, to the economy or to human health. Both halves are required.

paras.label: C
paras.text: So most introduced species are not invasive. Wheat is non-native almost everywhere it grows and nobody calls it an invader. The word is reserved for the small fraction that spread and damage something.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Harm is also where the arguments happen. A fish that wrecks a native fishery and supports a new commercial one is harmful by one measure and valuable by another, and which measure a report uses often tells you who paid for it.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The time limit is just as awkward. Horses were native to North America, went extinct there, and returned with Europeans, so whether a wild horse is a returning native or an introduction depends on where a person puts the line.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Biologists increasingly prefer a flatter phrase. Non-native, with the harm described separately and measured, says what the evidence supports without borrowing a word that assigns blame to an organism that merely arrived.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Invasive is a technical word with a military word inside it. The metaphor does real work. It suggests an attacker with a plan. A plant does not move that way.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The definition has two parts. A species must be non-native to the place. It must also cause harm there. Both halves are needed.

paras.label: C
paras.text: So most introduced species are not invasive. Wheat is non-native almost everywhere. Nobody calls wheat an invader. The word fits only the few that spread and damage.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Harm is where the arguments start. A fish may wreck one fishery and feed another. It is harmful by one measure and valuable by another. The measure often shows who paid for the report.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The time limit is awkward too. Horses were native to North America. They died out there. Europeans brought them back. So a wild horse may count either way.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Biologists now prefer a plainer phrase. They say non-native. Then they describe the harm separately. That says what the evidence supports.

questions.q: What two things must be true for a species to be called invasive?
questions.a: It must be non-native to the place, and it must cause harm there, to the ecosystem, to the economy or to human health.

questions.q: Paragraph A (i.e. the metaphor) and paragraph D (i.e. arguments about harm).
Summarize what invasive means and why biologists are moving away from the word.
questions.a: A species is invasive only if it is non-native and causes harm, so most introduced species, including wheat, do not qualify. Harm depends on who is measuring it and the cut-off for native is awkward, so biologists increasingly say non-native and describe the harm separately.

questions.q:
non-native: living in a place its species did not originally come from.
metaphor: a word borrowed from one thing to describe another, as invasive borrows from war.
Describe the connection between who paid for a report and how harm is measured in it.
questions.a: A fish can be harmful by one measure and valuable by another, so which measure a report uses often tells you who paid for it.

note: The connotation is the lesson, i.e. a word that "assigns blame to an organism that merely arrived." Ask what non-native loses as well as what it gains.

title: The Shape of a Science Article
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze how a particular sentence, paragraph, chapter, or section fits into the overall structure of a text and contributes to the development of the ideas.
 Spiral: RI.6.2 central idea · RI.6.3 development · RI.6.6 point of view · RI.6.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 770 – 870

paras.label: A
paras.text: A research paper looks like prose and works like a form. Every one has the same five parts in the same order, and a scientist reading it does not start at the beginning.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The abstract comes first and is written last. It is a compressed version of the whole paper, and most readers decide from it alone whether to read any further.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The introduction narrows. It opens with what the field already knows, moves to what it does not, and ends with the one question this paper will answer. A reader can usually find that question in the last sentence of the section.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Methods is the section nobody reads for pleasure and the one that decides whether the paper counts. It exists so that another lab can run the same study, and a method too vague to repeat is a finding that cannot be checked.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Results states what happened and nothing else. The discussion, which comes after, is where the authors are allowed to say what they think it means. Keeping those apart is the whole reason for the split.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The limitations paragraph sits near the end of the discussion. It is where the authors name what their study cannot show, and a paper without one is usually a paper making a larger claim than it earned.

paras.label: G
paras.text: So the order is an argument about trust. Each section does one job, the claims come after the evidence, and anything the authors want you to believe can be traced back to the part where they showed their work.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The abstract comes first. It is written last. It is a short version of the whole paper. Most readers stop there.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The introduction narrows. It starts with what the field knows. Then it names what the field does not know. The last sentence gives the question.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Methods is dull and it matters most. It lets another lab run the same study. A method too vague to repeat cannot be checked.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Results says what happened. That is all it says. The discussion comes next. There the authors may say what it means.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The limitations paragraph sits near the end. The authors name what their study cannot show. A paper without one is usually claiming too much.

paras.label: G
paras.text: So the order is about trust. Each section has one job. The claims come after the evidence.

questions.q: Why does the methods section matter even though nobody reads it for pleasure?
questions.a: It exists so that another lab can run the same study, and a method too vague to repeat is a finding that cannot be checked.

questions.q: Paragraph E (i.e. results against discussion) and paragraph F (i.e. limitations).
Summarize how a research paper is organized and why.
questions.a: It has five parts in a fixed order: an abstract written last, an introduction that narrows to one question, methods that let another lab repeat the study, results that state only what happened, and a discussion where the authors say what it means. The order keeps the claims after the evidence so a reader can check them.

questions.q:
abstract: the compressed version of a whole paper, placed first and written last.
limitations: the paragraph where authors name what their study cannot show.
Describe the connection between splitting results from discussion and what a reader can trust.
questions.a: Results states what happened and nothing else, and the discussion is where the authors are allowed to say what they think it means, so keeping those apart lets a reader separate the evidence from the interpretation.

note: This is RI.6.5 at the scale of a whole text. Ask which paragraph could move and which could not, i.e. why limitations cannot come before results.

title: The Turn in the Middle
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze how a particular sentence, paragraph, chapter, or section fits into the overall structure of a text and contributes to the development of the ideas.
 Spiral: RI.6.2 central idea · RI.6.3 development · RI.6.6 point of view · RI.6.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 770 – 870

paras.label: A
paras.text: Most arguments worth reading change direction once. The writer builds a case, then stops and takes the other side seriously, then answers it. That stop is the turn, and it usually arrives in the middle.

paras.label: B
paras.text: You can find it by its words. However, admittedly, it is true that, critics argue — each one announces that the next sentence will not continue the paragraph before it.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The turn is not a weakness. A reader who has already thought of the objection will stop trusting a writer who pretends it does not exist, so naming it first is what keeps them reading.

paras.label: D
paras.text: What the writer does after the turn is the test. A strong piece concedes the part that is actually true and then shows why the main claim survives anyway. A weak one restates the objection and calls it silly.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Remove the turn and the piece gets shorter and worse. It becomes a list of reasons for one side, which persuades nobody who did not already agree.

paras.label: F
paras.text: So when you read an argument, find the turn first. It tells you what the writer thinks the strongest case against them is, and whether they were willing to say it out loud.

paras.label: A
paras.text: Most good arguments change direction once. The writer builds a case. Then the writer takes the other side seriously. Then the writer answers it. That stop is the turn.

paras.label: B
paras.text: You can find it by its words. However. Admittedly. Critics argue. Each one warns you that the next sentence will not agree with the last.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The turn is not a weakness. A reader may have thought of the objection already. If the writer hides it, the reader stops trusting the writer.

paras.label: D
paras.text: What comes after the turn is the test. A strong piece admits the part that is true. Then it shows the main claim still holds. A weak piece just calls the objection silly.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Take out the turn and the piece gets worse. It becomes a list of reasons for one side. It persuades nobody.

paras.label: F
paras.text: So find the turn first. It shows what the writer fears most. It also shows whether they would say it out loud.

questions.q: What words signal that a turn is coming?
questions.a: However, admittedly, it is true that, and critics argue each announce that the next sentence will not continue the paragraph before it.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. why the turn builds trust) and paragraph D (i.e. what the writer does after it).
Summarize what the turn is and what it does for an argument.
questions.a: The turn is the point where a writer stops building their case, states the other side seriously, and answers it. It usually comes in the middle and is marked by words such as however or critics argue. Naming the objection keeps a reader who already thought of it, and what the writer does after the turn shows whether the argument is strong.

questions.q:
concede: to admit that part of the other side's case is true.
objection: the strongest reason somebody might disagree with the claim.
Describe the connection between hiding an objection and losing a reader.
questions.a: A reader who has already thought of the objection will stop trusting a writer who pretends it does not exist, so naming it first is what keeps them reading.

note: Have students mark the turn in a real opinion column. The piece with no turn in it is the one worth discussing.

title: Why the Timeline Comes First
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze how a particular sentence, paragraph, chapter, or section fits into the overall structure of a text and contributes to the development of the ideas.
 Spiral: RI.6.2 central idea · RI.6.3 development · RI.6.6 point of view · RI.6.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 770 – 870

paras.label: A
paras.text: Open a history chapter and the first thing on the page is usually a timeline. It is easy to skip, and skipping it is why the chapter gets harder three pages later.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A timeline does one job the prose cannot. It fixes the order of events in a single glance, so the reader is not holding dates in mind while also following an argument.

paras.label: C
paras.text: History writing rarely runs in order. A chapter may open in 1945, jump back thirty years for causes, and return. That structure is deliberate, and it only works if the reader has the straight sequence somewhere to check against.

paras.label: E
paras.text: What a timeline leaves out is the argument. It will tell you that two things happened in order and never that one caused the other, and a reader who treats sequence as cause has misread it.

paras.label: F

title: Where a Lab Report Ends
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze how a particular sentence, paragraph, chapter, or section fits into the overall structure of a text and contributes to the development of the ideas.
 Spiral: RI.6.2 central idea · RI.6.3 development · RI.6.6 point of view · RI.6.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 770 – 870

paras.label: A
paras.text: Students are often taught that a lab report ends with a conclusion, and then taught to write the conclusion as a summary. Those two instructions pull in opposite directions.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A summary repeats. A conclusion decides. The last section of a report is where the writer answers the question the first section asked, and a reader should be able to read those two paragraphs alone and understand the point.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Which means the conclusion is written against the hypothesis, not against the data. If the opening predicted that the salt water would freeze later, the ending says whether it did, in those words.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The sentence that makes a conclusion work is usually the one admitting what went wrong. A thermometer read in a warm room, a timer started late — naming it is not a confession, it is the reason the number came out as it did.

paras.label: E
paras.text: A conclusion that ends with what to do next is stronger than one that ends with a result. The next experiment is the evidence that the writer understood their own.

paras.label: F
paras.text: So the shape is a circle. The question at the front and the answer at the back hold the report together, and everything between them is there to get from one to the other.

conclusion: the section that decides the question rather than repeating the report.

questions.a: The last section answers the question the first section asked, so the question at the front and the answer at the back hold the report together and everything between them is there to get from one to the other.

title: The Sidebar and the Story
standard_text:
Standard: Analyze how a particular sentence, paragraph, chapter, or section fits into the overall structure of a text and contributes to the development of the ideas.
 Spiral: RI.6.2 central idea · RI.6.3 development · RI.6.6 point of view · RI.6.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 770 – 870

paras.label: A
paras.text: A news feature often carries a box beside the main text, set in a different typeface and a tinted panel. The box is not an interruption. It is doing work the article cannot do without stopping.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The main story has to move. A sidebar holds the material that would break that movement: a definition, a short history, the numbers behind a claim, a second voice that does not fit the narrative.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Where it sits is a decision. A sidebar placed beside the paragraph it serves gets read; the same box at the end of the article usually does not, and editors argue about this.

paras.label: D
paras.text: A sidebar can also carry the part the writer is least sure of. A disputed figure, a claim from one source only — putting it in a box marks it as separate from the reporting without hiding it.

paras.label: E
paras.text: That means reading the box changes the article. A story about a factory closing reads one way beside a sidebar on the town's unemployment rate and another beside one on the owner's other plants.

paras.label: F
paras.text: So the question to ask is not what the sidebar says but why it is a sidebar. Something was kept out of the main column on purpose, and what it was tells you how the writer wanted the story to run.

title: Who Wrote the Brochure
standard_text:
Standard: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text and explain how it is conveyed in the text.
 Spiral: RI.6.1 citing evidence · RI.6.4 word meaning · RI.6.8 claims and evidence · RI.6.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 770 – 870

paras.label: A
paras.text: A national park brochure and a resort brochure for the same valley can both be accurate and leave opposite impressions. Neither has to lie to do it, and neither usually does.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Start with who paid. The park service brochure is funded by an agency whose job is protecting the place and whose budget depends on visitors behaving. The resort's is funded by somebody selling rooms.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The park brochure warns. It names the elevation, the afternoon storms, the distance to the nearest water, and the two trails that have killed people. Warning you is part of its purpose.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The resort brochure photographs the same trail in good light and does not mention the storms. Everything in it is true, and the storms are missing, and that absence is the point.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Word choice carries the rest. One says rugged and remote; the other says secluded and unspoiled. They are describing the same emptiness and asking you to feel differently about it.

paras.label: F
paras.text: So the question is not which brochure is honest. Both can be. It is what each one needs you to do after reading it — stay safe, or book a room — and every choice in it follows from that.

purpose: what a text is trying to get the reader to think or do.

Describe the connection between who paid for a brochure and what it leaves out.
questions.a: The resort's brochure is funded by somebody selling rooms, so it does not mention the storms, while the park service brochure is funded by an agency whose job is protecting the place and warning you is part of its purpose.

note: Paragraph E is the cleanest pair of synonyms students will meet all year, i.e. "rugged and remote" against "secluded and unspoiled." Same fact, opposite feeling.

title: The Scientist and the Press Release
standard_text:
Standard: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text and explain how it is conveyed in the text.
 Spiral: RI.6.1 citing evidence · RI.6.4 word meaning · RI.6.8 claims and evidence · RI.6.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 770 – 870

paras.label: A
paras.text: A study is published, a university writes a press release about it, and a news site writes a story from the release. By the end of that chain the claim is often larger than the study.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The study is written to be careful. It says that an association was observed in a sample of a particular size, under particular conditions, and that further work is needed.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The press release is written to be noticed. It is produced by a communications office whose purpose is attention for the university, and its first sentence usually drops the conditions.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Researchers do not always see it before it goes out, and some have publicly objected to the version of their own work that ended up in the headline.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The news story then works from the release rather than the paper. Studies of this chain have found that most of the exaggeration in health reporting is already present in the release, not added by the journalist.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The tells are findable. A study says may be associated with; a release says could help prevent; a headline says prevents. Each step drops a hedge and nobody writes anything untrue.

paras.label: G
paras.text: So read in the other direction. Find the study, read what it says it measured and in how many people, and compare that to the sentence that reached you.

hedge: a word that limits a claim, such as may or associated with.
press release: an announcement written by an organization's own communications office.
Describe the connection between the purpose of a communications office and the first sentence of a release.
questions.a: Its purpose is attention for the university, so the first sentence usually drops the conditions the study was careful to state.

note: Paragraph F is a three-step ladder worth putting on the board, i.e. "may be associated with" to "could help prevent" to "prevents."

title: A Letter to the Editor About the Dam
standard_text:
Standard: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text and explain how it is conveyed in the text.
 Spiral: RI.6.1 citing evidence · RI.6.4 word meaning · RI.6.8 claims and evidence · RI.6.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 770 – 870

paras.label: A
paras.text: A letter in a small-town paper argues that the old dam should stay. It runs four hundred words and never says what the writer does for a living. It is signed with a name and a street.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The argument is about memory. The writer swam in that reservoir as a child, names three families who did the same, and asks what the town will be without it.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Not one sentence addresses the engineering report. The report says the spillway has failed inspection twice, and the letter does not mention a spillway at all.

paras.label: D
paras.text: That silence is the strongest clue to purpose. A writer who wanted to win on the merits would take on the report; a writer who wants the reader to feel something will stay where the feeling is.

paras.label: E
paras.text: It can still be worth reading. What the town loses is real, and it is a thing the engineering report does not measure and was never meant to.

paras.label: F
paras.text: So hold both. The letter is evidence about what people value and no evidence at all about whether the dam is safe. Treating it as either one alone gets the decision wrong, and only one of the two questions is one an engineer can answer.
