title: Why the Museum Label Says Probably
standard_text:
Standard: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text and explain how it is conveyed in the text.
 Spiral: RI.6.1 citing evidence · RI.6.4 word meaning · RI.6.8 claims and evidence · RI.6.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 770 – 870

paras.label: A
paras.text: A museum label is about forty words long and every one of them has been argued over. The hedges in it are not caution for its own sake. They are a record of how much is actually known.

paras.label: B
paras.text: Probably a burial site means the objects were found arranged the way burials usually are, and no body survived. Ritual object means nobody knows what it was for.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Attributed to means the museum is not certain who made it. Circle of means somebody in that workshop. After means a later copy. Each is a different distance from the artist's own hand.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Date ranges work the same way. 1480 to 1520 is not vagueness; it is the span the evidence allows, and narrowing it would be claiming more than the museum can support.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The labels also record how an object arrived. Acquired in 1897 and collected during the expedition are doing different work, and some museums now say removed from, which is a sentence about a dispute.

paras.label: F
paras.text: So read the hedges as the honest part. A label with no qualifiers anywhere is either very well evidenced or written by somebody who has stopped distinguishing what is known from what is assumed.

title: The Company's Report on the River
standard_text:
Standard: Determine an author's point of view or purpose in a text and explain how it is conveyed in the text.
 Spiral: RI.6.1 citing evidence · RI.6.4 word meaning · RI.6.8 claims and evidence · RI.6.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 770 – 870

paras.label: A
paras.text: When a plant is accused of polluting a river, three reports usually appear. The company writes one, the state agency writes one, and a university lab writes one, and all three may use the same samples.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The company's report is not required to lie and generally does not. It selects. It reports the readings downstream of the outfall after the spring melt, when the river is highest and anything in it is most dilute.

paras.label: C
paras.text: It also chooses the comparison. Measured against the legal limit, the number passes. Measured against the river above the plant, the same number is eleven times higher.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The agency report is bound by a procedure, which is its strength and its limit. It tests what the rules say to test, on the schedule the rules set, which a plant can plan around.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The university lab has the most freedom and the least power. It can sample where it likes and publish what it finds, and it cannot require anybody to do anything about it.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Who funded each one is printed somewhere in all three, usually near the back. It does not tell you which is wrong. It tells you which questions each was built to answer.

paras.label: G
paras.text: So compare the methods sections before the conclusions. Where they sampled, when, and what they compared it to will explain most of the disagreement before you reach anybody's opinion.

title: The Graph and the Glacier
standard_text:
Standard: Integrate information presented in different media or formats, including visually and quantitatively, as well as in words to develop a coherent understanding of a topic or issue.
 Spiral: RI.6.1 citing evidence · RI.6.2 central idea · RI.6.9 comparing accounts · RI.6.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 770 – 870

paras.label: A
paras.text: A photograph of a glacier taken in 1920 beside one from today is the most persuasive thing in any article about ice. It is also the least precise, and the two facts are related.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The photographs show that the front of the glacier has moved. They cannot say how fast, when most of it happened, or whether it is still happening. A century is a long gap between two frames.

paras.label: C

title: A Map, a Table, and a Flood
standard_text:
Standard: Integrate information presented in different media or formats, including visually and quantitatively, as well as in words to develop a coherent understanding of a topic or issue.

paras.label: A
paras.text: After a river floods, a town meeting usually has three documents on the table, and they do not agree about who was hurt.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The map shades the flooded area. It is the only one that shows where, and it treats every shaded house the same, whether the water came to the doorstep or the ceiling.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The table counts. Houses damaged, dollars claimed, days out of the home — it distinguishes severity, and it has no geography at all, so you cannot see that one street took most of it.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The photographs do what neither can. A single picture of a kitchen under four feet of water puts a number into a body, and it also shows one kitchen out of six hundred.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The disagreement is usually about scale. The map says twelve percent of the town flooded. The table says the average claim was eleven thousand dollars. Both are true and neither mentions that twenty families lost everything.

paras.label: F
paras.text: So the question for the meeting is which document the decision is being made from. A budget drawn from the average will not reach the twenty, and a budget drawn from the photograph will not reach the rest.

title: Reading a Population Pyramid
standard_text:
Standard: Integrate information presented in different media or formats, including visually and quantitatively, as well as in words to develop a coherent understanding of a topic or issue.
 Spiral: RI.6.1 citing evidence · RI.6.2 central idea · RI.6.9 comparing accounts · RI.6.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 770 – 870

paras.label: A
paras.text: A population pyramid is two bar charts laid back to back, men on one side and women on the other, with age rising from the bottom. The shape alone tells you most of what a country is about to face.

paras.label: B
paras.text: A wide base and a narrow top means many children and few old people. Those countries need schools now and will need jobs in fifteen years, and they can usually say exactly when.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A narrow base under a thick middle is the opposite problem. Japan's pyramid is shaped like a lightbulb, and every worker there supports a growing number of retired people.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Notches are history. A pinch in one age band marks a war, a famine, or a policy, and because that band also had fewer children, the pinch reappears twenty-five years higher up.

paras.label: E
paras.text: What a pyramid cannot show is movement. Migration in and out is invisible on it, which is why a country's pyramid and its actual population can diverge within a decade.

paras.label: F
paras.text: So read the shape, then the notches, then the year it was drawn. A pyramid is a photograph of a population, and the thing it is best at is telling you what happens next.

title: The Chart in the Doctor's Office
standard_text:
Standard: Integrate information presented in different media or formats, including visually and quantitatively, as well as in words to develop a coherent understanding of a topic or issue.
 Spiral: RI.6.1 citing evidence · RI.6.2 central idea · RI.6.9 comparing accounts · RI.6.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 770 – 870

paras.label: A
paras.text: A growth chart is a sheet of curved lines, and a child's height is a dot somewhere among them. Parents read the dot. Doctors read which line it is following.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The lines are percentiles. A child on the fiftieth is taller than half of children that age; one on the fifth is taller than one in twenty. None of those is a grade, and the chart does not have a passing line.

paras.label: C
paras.text: A dot low on the chart is not the concern. A child who has tracked the tenth percentile since birth is growing exactly as expected, and the expected thing is to stay on your line.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Crossing lines is what gets attention. A child who moves from the fiftieth to the tenth over two years has not become short; something has changed, and the chart found it because two dots were compared and not just read.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The chart also only works for what it was built from. Different charts exist for different populations and for premature infants, and using the wrong one produces a worrying dot and no actual problem.

paras.label: F
paras.text: So the useful object is not the dot. It is the line of dots across years, which is why the nurse measures a child who has obviously grown and writes it down anyway.

title: The Seismograph and the Map
standard_text:
Standard: Integrate information presented in different media or formats, including visually and quantitatively, as well as in words to develop a coherent understanding of a topic or issue.
 Spiral: RI.6.1 citing evidence · RI.6.2 central idea · RI.6.9 comparing accounts · RI.6.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 770 – 870

paras.label: A
paras.text: An earthquake arrives at a seismograph as a wiggle on a line, and the wiggle is not a picture of the shaking. It is a record of two different waves arriving at two different times.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The fast wave comes first. P waves travel through rock at about six kilometers a second; S waves follow at roughly half that, and the gap between them on the trace is the only thing needed to find the distance.

paras.label: C
paras.text: That gives a distance, not a direction. A single station can say the quake was two hundred kilometers away and nothing more, which draws a circle of possible locations around it.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Three stations give a point. Three circles cross in one place, and that intersection is the epicenter, which is why a seismic network is useless with one instrument and precise with several.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The height of the wiggle is a separate measurement. Amplitude gives magnitude, and magnitude is a number about the quake itself rather than about how it felt anywhere in particular.

paras.label: F
paras.text: How it felt is a different map. Shaking intensity is collected from instruments and from people reporting what moved, and it depends on soil, depth and building type as much as on magnitude.

paras.label: G
paras.text: So a magnitude 6 is one number and the intensity map is a thousand. Reading only the number tells you what happened at the fault; reading only the map tells you nothing about what the fault did.

title: Should the City Build a Bike Lane?
standard_text:
Standard: Trace and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, distinguishing claims that are supported by reasons and evidence from claims that are not.
 Spiral: RI.6.1 citing evidence · RI.6.5 structure · RI.6.6 point of view · RI.6.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 770 – 870

paras.label: A
paras.text: The proposal would take one of four traffic lanes on Market Street and make it a protected bike lane. The council packet runs eleven pages. Four of its claims carry evidence and three do not.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The supported ones are easy to check. The city counted 1,340 cyclists a day on Market Street in September, and the fire department's own letter says a protected lane does not narrow the path for an engine.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The crash figure is supported and smaller than it sounds. Collisions involving cyclists fell 38 percent on Oak Street after its lane was built, which is six fewer crashes a year on one street over three years.

paras.label: D
paras.text: Three claims have nothing behind them. The packet says the lane will bring shoppers downtown, that property values will rise, and that traffic will not get worse. No study, no comparison city, no figure.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The last of those is the one to press. Taking a lane away and expecting no change in traffic is a claim that could be tested, cheaply, by measuring Oak Street before and after. Nobody did.

paras.label: F
paras.text: An argument can be worth supporting and badly made at the same time. The cyclist count and the fire department letter are reasons. The property values are a hope with a sentence around it.

title: The Claim That Sharks Do Not Get Cancer
standard_text:
Standard: Trace and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, distinguishing claims that are supported by reasons and evidence from claims that are not.
 Spiral: RI.6.1 citing evidence · RI.6.5 structure · RI.6.6 point of view · RI.6.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 770 – 870

paras.label: A
paras.text: A 1992 book called Sharks Don't Get Cancer sold well and built an industry. Shark cartilage pills were being sold for hundreds of dollars a bottle within a few years.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The argument ran in three steps. Sharks do not get cancer; their skeletons are cartilage; therefore cartilage prevents cancer. Each step was offered as support for the next.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The first step is false. The Registry of Tumors in Lower Animals has documented dozens of tumors in sharks, including cancers of the cartilage itself, which were on record before the book was written.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The second step is true and does no work. Sharks do have cartilage skeletons, and that fact supports nothing about cancer unless the first step holds.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The third step does not follow even if the first two did. A substance in an animal's body is not a drug you can swallow; cartilage is mostly protein, and protein is digested rather than delivered.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Trials settled it. Controlled studies of shark cartilage in patients with advanced cancer found no benefit, and regulators have acted against companies for claiming otherwise.

paras.label: G
paras.text: The cost was not only money. Shark populations were fished down for the pills, and some patients took them instead of treatment that worked.

title: Is Bottled Water Worth It?
standard_text:
Standard: Trace and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, distinguishing claims that are supported by reasons and evidence from claims that are not.

paras.label: A
paras.text: A flyer handed out at a school fair argues that families should stop buying bottled water. It makes five claims, and the strong ones are not the loud ones.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The cost claim is solid. A gallon from the tap costs a fraction of a cent in most American cities, and the same gallon in bottles runs a few dollars, which is a comparison anyone can check on a bill.

paras.label: C
paras.text: The safety claim is weaker than the flyer suggests. Municipal water in the United States is tested more often than bottled water is, which is true, and that does not make every tap safe — Flint had tested water and a lead problem.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The plastic claim is supported and overstated. Bottles really do take centuries to break down, and the flyer's figure of ninety-one percent unrecycled is a global number quoted as if it were local.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The taste claim is not an argument. Whether tap water tastes worse varies by city and by person, and the flyer offers it as though it settled something.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The one missing piece is the exception. Some people cannot drink their tap water, and a flyer that never says so is making a weaker case than it could, because it leaves itself one obvious counterexample.

title: The Advertisement for the Memory Pill

Standard: Trace and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, distinguishing claims that are supported by reasons and evidence from claims that are not.
 Spiral: RI.6.1 citing evidence · RI.6.5 structure · RI.6.6 point of view · RI.6.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 770 – 870

paras.label: A
paras.text: A full-page advertisement promises better memory in thirty days. It reads like an argument and is built out of things that are not evidence.

paras.label: B
paras.text: It opens with a doctor. The photograph is of a person in a white coat, the name has letters after it, and nothing says what the letters are or whether the person studied memory.

paras.label: C
paras.text: Then come the testimonials. Four people say the pill worked, and a testimonial cannot show that a pill works because nobody collected the people it did nothing for.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The study it cites is real and the sentence about it is not. The advertisement says clinically proven; the study had eleven participants, no comparison group, and ran for two weeks.

paras.label: E
paras.text: The graph has no numbers on the vertical axis. The bars rise, and without units a rising bar can represent any difference at all, including none worth noticing.

paras.label: F
paras.text: The small print carries the actual claim. These statements have not been evaluated by the Food and Drug Administration, it says, and that sentence contradicts the headline above it.

paras.label: G
paras.text: So the test is not whether an argument sounds like science. It is whether any part of it could come out the other way, and nothing in this advertisement could.

questions.q: Why can a testimonial not show that a pill works?
questions.a: Nobody collected the people it did nothing for, so four people saying it worked does not show that the pill worked.

questions.q: Paragraph D (i.e. what the study actually was) and paragraph F (i.e. the small print).
Summarize how the advertisement is built and why none of it is evidence.
questions.a: It opens with a white coat and letters after a name that are never explained, offers four testimonials with no account of anyone it failed, calls a study of eleven people with no comparison group clinically proven, and prints a graph with no units. The small print then says the statements have not been evaluated at all.

questions.q:
testimonial: one person's account of a product working, offered in place of a trial.
comparison group: the people in a study who do not get the treatment, so the effect can be measured against something.
Describe the connection between the small print and the headline.
questions.a: The small print says these statements have not been evaluated by the Food and Drug Administration, and that sentence contradicts the headline above it.

note: Paragraph G is the transferable test, i.e. "whether any part of it could come out the other way." An argument that cannot fail is not an argument.

title: Should the Dam Come Down?
standard_text:
Standard: Trace and evaluate the argument and specific claims in a text, distinguishing claims that are supported by reasons and evidence from claims that are not.
 Spiral: RI.6.1 citing evidence · RI.6.5 structure · RI.6.6 point of view · RI.6.10 comprehension
 Lower range: LL 770 – 870

paras.label: A
paras.text: Two sides filed written statements with the county about an eighty-year-old dam, and both are arguing honestly from different things they can prove.

paras.label: B
paras.text: The removal side has the fish numbers. Salmon counts above four comparable removed dams rose within three years, with figures from state surveys attached to the filing.

paras.label: C
paras.text: They also claim the dam is unsafe, and that one is borrowed. It rests on a state inspection of a different dam built the same decade, which is a reason to inspect this one and not a finding about it.

paras.label: D
paras.text: The keep side has the water. Sixty homes draw from the reservoir, and the engineering study they attached shows what each would pay to connect to the municipal line.

paras.label: E
paras.text: Their second claim is the weak one. They say removal will flood downstream property, and the filing offers no model, no comparable case, and no figure — the opposite of what their first claim did.

paras.label: F
paras.text: Both sides leave out the same thing. Neither filing says what happens if nothing is done, although the dam will keep aging either way and doing nothing is the option that requires no vote.

paras.label: G
paras.text: So the strongest claim on each side is specific and local, and the weakest on each side is general and borrowed. That pattern is worth more than knowing which side you are on.

questions.q: What evidence does the removal side attach?
questions.a: Salmon counts above four comparable removed dams rose within three years, with figures from state surveys attached to the filing.

questions.q: Paragraph C (i.e. the borrowed safety claim) and paragraph E (i.e. the flooding claim with no figure).
Summarize the strongest and weakest claim on each side.
questions.a: The removal side has salmon counts from four comparable dams with state surveys attached, and a borrowed safety claim resting on an inspection of a different dam. The keep side has an engineering study of what sixty homes would pay to connect to the city line, and an unsupported claim that removal will flood downstream property.

questions.q:
filing: a written statement submitted formally to a government body.
borrowed evidence: a finding about a different case offered as though it were about this one.
Describe the connection between how specific a claim is and how well it is supported.
questions.a: The strongest claim on each side is specific and local and the weakest on each side is general and borrowed, which is the pattern worth noticing.

note: Paragraph F is the move most students miss. Doing nothing is an option on the table and neither filing argues against it.
